name: Primary lateral sclerosis
aliases: primary lateral sclerosis of the motor neurone disease spectrum

reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Presents with a slowly progressive, symmetrical spastic paraparesis that often begins in the legs and ascends, later involving the arms and bulbar muscles
Signs are those of pure upper motor neurone dysfunction: spasticity, hyperreflexia, extensor plantar responses, and a spastic dysarthria, without significant wasting or fasciculation
By convention a diagnosis is favoured when there is no clinical or electrophysiological evidence of lower motor neurone involvement after a prolonged period, commonly around four years
A pseudobulbar affect with emotional lability is frequent and reflects bilateral corticobulbar tract involvement
Disease course is far more indolent than amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and survival is measured in decades rather than years
Bladder urgency from a spastic bladder may develop, but sensory loss and prominent muscle atrophy should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis
A proportion of apparently pure upper motor neurone cases eventually declare lower motor neurone signs and are reclassified within the amyotrophic lateral sclerosis spectrum
reference.pathophysiology: Primary lateral sclerosis is a rare degenerative disorder confined largely to the upper motor neurones, with selective loss of the large Betz cells of the primary motor cortex and degeneration of the corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts. Unlike amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, the anterior horn cells and lower motor neurones are relatively spared, at least for a prolonged period, which explains the predominance of spasticity over wasting. The condition is regarded as sitting at the upper motor neurone end of the motor neurone disease spectrum, and its precise molecular basis remains uncertain, although overlap with familial motor neurone disease genes is recognised in some cases.
additionalDifferentials: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis with predominant upper motor neurone signs
Cervical spondylotic myelopathy or other compressive myelopathy
Multiple sclerosis with a progressive myelopathic course
Subacute combined degeneration from vitamin B12 deficiency
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the brain and whole spine to exclude compressive, demyelinating and structural lesions
Electromyography and nerve conduction studies to demonstrate absence of lower motor neurone denervation
Serum vitamin B12, copper and very-long-chain fatty acids to exclude metabolic myelopathies
HTLV-1 serology where exposure risk exists
Genetic testing for hereditary spastic paraparesis genes when a familial pattern is suspected
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis to help exclude inflammatory or infective myelopathy
redFlags: Emergence of muscle wasting, fasciculation or a positive electromyogram, indicating conversion to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
A clear sensory level or sphincter disturbance suggesting a structural cord lesion
Rapidly progressive weakness inconsistent with the expected indolent course
Bulbar dysfunction causing unsafe swallowing and aspiration risk
reference.prognosis: Primary lateral sclerosis progresses slowly over many years and is associated with a much longer survival than amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, although accumulating spasticity and eventual bulbar involvement cause substantial disability; a subset later develop lower motor neurone signs and are reclassified.
pitfalls: Diagnosing primary lateral sclerosis too early, before enough time has elapsed to exclude conversion to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
Overlooking a compressive cervical myelopathy that can mimic pure upper motor neurone disease
Attributing emotional lability to a mood disorder rather than recognising pseudobulbar affect
Missing a treatable metabolic or hereditary cause of progressive spastic paraparesis
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
